p: The name joins two Sanskrit words, dakshina, south, and patha, road. The later Vedic texts divide the Indian subcontinent into three parts: Aryavarta in the north, Madhya Desha in the centre and Dakshinapatha in the south. The Aitareya Brahmana, of the first half of the first millennium BCE, names peoples of the south of Vindhyan and north Deccan origin, among them the Satvants, Vidarbha, Andhra, Nishadas and Kuntis. The grammarian Panini, about 500 BCE, mentions the Asmaka Kingdom in connection with the south and with Kalinga.

The term has carried three meanings. It can denote the ancient south of the subcontinent below Uttarapatha, usually the Deccan and sometimes Tamilakam and Ceylon as well. It can mean the great southern highway, running from Magadha to Pratishthana. It has also been used for a kingdom on the Godavari River. The Junagarh rock inscription of 150 CE, set up by an Indo-Scythian king, records that he twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight and did not destroy him because of the nearness of their connection.

The southern road was one of two great highways that have linked the parts of the subcontinent since the Iron Age. The other, the Uttarapatha or great northern road, ran from Taxila through the Punjab to the Yamuna and followed that river south to Mathura; from there a route went on to Ujjain in Malwa and to Broach on the western coast. According to the writer Sanjeev Sanyal, the course of the northern road has stayed roughly the same since before the Mauryas, while the southern road appears to have drifted.

The route of Rama into exile in the epic may reflect an early version of it. By the time of the Buddha it started at Varanasi and ran through Vidisha in central India to Pratishthana, now Paithan, and it probably extended to the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the far south. By the Mauryan period there would have been a branch from Ujjain to the ports of Gujarat, which made Ujjain a major city by the Gupta era. The modern highway that roughly corresponds to it runs much further east than the old road but still meets the northern road at Varanasi.

notes: The article names the Junagarh inscription's king 'Rudradharman'; the usual form is Rudradaman. Unsure which the site uses, I wrote 'an Indo-Scythian king' without the name. Add the name if you can confirm it.

The existing description says the road linked Shravasti and Ujjain with Pratishthana; the article says Magadha to Pratishthana (lead) and Varanasi-Vidisha-Pratishthana (Sanyal). I followed the article; Shravasti is not in it.
The article is thin (about 450 words of substance), so the entry is at the short end. Modern highway numbers (NH 44 etc.) left out.
